notes: Edition composed by Claude from the collected headlines, reading titles and metadata only.
Each narrative is an idea that joins several different events; what it joins is listed at the top. It commits to a claim, and the last rung of every narrative is the case against it. Read both.

Each narrative ends with 'How we got here': four horizons, the past decade, the past fifty years, since September 2001 and since 1945, that place the day's pattern on longer trajectories. They are a trajectory, not a verdict.
The connections are made by the model, not by the publishers. Follow any headline to the original report before repeating it.
Books and trajectories appear only where they change how a fragment or a horizon reads.

readings.line: The Iran war's fuel squeeze reaches US air fares, easyJet luggage, Estonian asphalt and Malaysian subsidies
readings.claim: The fuel squeeze from the Iran war, which the previous edition followed at the petrol pump, now shows up in products refined from oil and in the rules governments use to price them. Fortune reports US airlines charging about 23% more for emptier planes after jet fuel rose more than 90%. An easyJet flight left Naples for Berlin without luggage for lack of fuel, and Estonia ran out of asphalt when bitumen supplies were disrupted, while Malaysia, India, Ukraine and South Korea adjust fuel formulas, blending caps, electricity incentives and reactor licences. The join matters because the cost has moved from drivers to anyone who flies, builds roads, borrows money or depends on a state subsidy.

events.label: US airlines raise fares for emptier planes
easyJet flight leaves Naples without luggage
Estonia runs out of asphalt
Governments revise fuel and power rules
Fuel costs enter elections and interest rates
Gas and diesel diplomacy around Hormuz

fragments.label: Air fares and empty seats
fragments.text: Fortune reports that US airlines are charging nearly 23% more for tickets and flying emptier planes, after jet fuel prices rose more than 90% in what it calls the Iran war's fuel squeeze. The headline describes airlines choosing fewer passengers at higher fares rather than absorbing the cost.

fragments.label: A flight without bags
fragments.text: Il Messaggero reports an easyJet flight from Naples to Berlin that departed without passengers' luggage for lack of fuel, with the airline citing problems due to a strike. Leaving baggage behind is what an airline does when it can load less fuel than planned and must cut weight.

fragments.label: Estonia's roads
fragments.text: Izvestia reports that Estonia has run out of asphalt because supplies of bitumen have been disrupted. Bitumen is the heavy residue of oil refining that binds road surfaces, a use of oil that rarely appears in stories about fuel prices.

fragments.label: Formulas, caps and cashback
fragments.text: The Star reports that Malaysia is studying a phased automatic fuel price adjustment from 2027. The Times of India quotes the petroleum minister Hardeep Puri saying India has no plans to raise ethanol blending beyond 20% for now. UNIAN reports experts expecting a new cashback scheme to reward Ukrainians for saving electricity.

fragments.label: A reactor kept running
fragments.text: Newspim reports that South Korea's nuclear operator KHNP has approved continued operation of Gori units 3 and 4 and is preparing a restart. The headline does not mention oil, but Korea imports almost all of its fuel and is extending the life of plants that reduce that need.

fragments.label: Supply around Hormuz
fragments.text: Al Jazeera reports that Tehran has completed a gas repair package and threatens to cut supplies to major consumers, and the Jerusalem Post reports Qatar urging Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Lenta.RU reports the US Department of Energy explaining a diesel deal with Russia. The fuels being chased are gas and refined products as much as crude, which is why the shortages appear first at airports and road depots.

fragments.label: One cause, four points of contact
fragments.text: Air fares in the US, a baggage decision in Naples, road surfacing in Estonia and a pricing formula in Malaysia share one upstream cause in the war's fuel squeeze. Each sits at a different point between the refinery and the user. Each passes the cost to a different person: the passenger, the traveller without bags, the road builder and the taxpayer who funds the subsidy.

fragments.label: Voters and borrowers
fragments.text: Fortune reports US consumers paying nearly eight times more than anyone else in fuel costs, and the National Post in Canada runs a column blaming governments for high gas prices. Financial News in Korea reports American voters saying the Iran war raised living costs a week before the midterms. The Reserve Bank of India's deputy governor says growth could have passed 8% without external shocks, CNBC's survey says Fed rate rises are coming and Yicai reports US Treasury yields at a twenty-year high. The fuel cost is now an argument in elections and in the price of borrowing.

fragments.label: Other causes for Naples and Estonia
fragments.text: The two most unusual items do not name the Iran war. Il Messaggero attributes the easyJet problem to a strike, which could be a local dispute at a fuel supplier in Naples unrelated to world prices. Izvestia, a Russian paper, has its own reasons to report shortages in an EU state that stopped buying from Russia, and Estonia's asphalt gap may come from one refinery or one shipping problem.

fragments.label: Ordinary policy read as shock
fragments.text: Malaysia's pricing review, India's ethanol limit and Korea's reactor licence each have long domestic histories in subsidy budgets, car engines, sugar supply and safety reviews of ageing plants. Reading them as responses to this month's fuel price attaches every energy decision to the war. The collection also leans on US business outlets such as Fortune and CNBC, which frame the shock in American terms.

horizons.label: How we got here: the past ten years
horizons.text: In September 2019 drones and missiles hit the Abqaiq processing plant and cut Saudi oil output by about half for several days, showing that Gulf energy sites could be struck cheaply from far away. After Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, the tightest markets were diesel and jet fuel rather than crude, and the EU ban on Russian refined products from February 2023 sent European importers to refineries further away, in the Gulf and India among them. Governments that had promised stable pump prices took on more of the cost. India reached 20% ethanol blending in 2025, five years ahead of its original target, partly to import less oil. The American strikes on Fordow in June 2025 ended a twelve-day war but left the Strait of Hormuz as the unresolved question. By these headlines the war has resumed, jet fuel has risen more than 90% and Malaysia is studying an automatic price formula from 2027. Across the decade importers learned that refined products tighten before crude does, which is the condition behind an easyJet flight leaving Naples without its bags.

horizons.label: How we got here: the past fifty years
horizons.text: The Arab oil embargo of October 1973 quadrupled the price of crude within months and taught importers that a regional war could become a domestic price. The answers chosen then are the policies these headlines report being adjusted now. Brazil launched its Proálcool ethanol programme in 1975, the model behind blending targets such as the 20% cap India's petroleum minister defends. Rich importers founded the International Energy Agency in 1974 and built strategic oil stocks. South Korea, with almost no oil of its own, opened its first reactor at Kori in 1978; the Newspim headline about continued operation of Gori units 3 and 4 concerns the same site under a different spelling. The Iranian revolution of 1979 brought a second price shock and drew the alliance lines still visible in Qatar's appeal to Iran to reopen Hormuz. Daniel Yergin's The Prize tells this as the story of states learning that oil is a strategic material. The account is contested by those who argue that markets, not stocks or reactors, ended the shocks, when the price collapsed in 1986.

horizons.label: How we got here: since September 2001
horizons.text: Oil reached a record of about $147 a barrel in July 2008, two months before Lehman Brothers failed, and fell below $40 by the end of that year. The swing taught airlines to hedge fuel and governments to reconsider fixed pump prices. American shale output then rose so fast that by 2020 the United States was a net exporter of petroleum, which is the background to Fortune's complaint that US consumers now pay far more in fuel costs than anyone else: a producing country whose prices still follow the world market. When crude fell in late 2014, Malaysia replaced its fixed petrol subsidy with a managed float, and the Star's report of an automatic adjustment from 2027 returns to that choice. After 2021 energy prices fed inflation and the Federal Reserve raised rates from near zero in 2022. By these headlines, CNBC's survey expects further Fed rises and US Treasury yields have reached a twenty-year high, so the fuel shock reaches borrowers as well as drivers and passengers.

horizons.label: How we got here: since 1945
horizons.text: On 14 February 1945 Roosevelt and Ibn Saud met on a cruiser in the Great Bitter Lake and agreed, without a written text, that American protection would accompany Saudi oil. The postwar economy was built on cheap Gulf crude moving by sea. The Suez crisis of 1956 closed the canal for months and showed that one narrow passage could raise costs across Europe; the canal closed again from 1967 to 1975. In the same years flying became a mass industry on the assumption of cheap kerosene. The 1944 Chicago Convention kept fuel carried on international flights free of customs duty, and the Boeing 707 entered service in 1958. Budget airlines such as easyJet, founded in 1995, took that assumption furthest, selling seats near cost and filling every plane. Fortune's report that US airlines now accept emptier planes in exchange for fares about 23% higher shows the model reversing when the fuel price does. Hormuz has replaced Suez as the passage in question, but the structure of one strait and many dependent economies dates from 1945.

readings.line: The US figures in Flávio Bolsonaro's exit, Lula's sovereignty warning, Colombian drills and Machado's return
readings.claim: After Lula's victory in Brazil's run-off, the United States is the common party in Latin American stories that are otherwise separate. Flávio Bolsonaro is reported travelling to the US with talk of asylum from Trump, Lula warns of persecution and promises to defend sovereignty, about 300 US soldiers arrive in Colombia for anti-drug exercises, and Corina Machado's return to Venezuela is read in Buenos Aires as a test of US influence. The previous edition covered Trump calling the Brazilian vote rigged before the result; the change is that Washington now appears as a destination for the losing side and as a military presence next door. That places part of the defeated Brazilian right's future, and some of the region's domestic quarrels, in the hands of a foreign government.

events.label: Flávio Bolsonaro leaves for the US
Other Bolsonaristas abroad or conceding
Lula warns of persecution and foreign money
US soldiers arrive in Colombia
Machado returns to Venezuela
Korean paper sees check on US doctrine

fragments.label: Reports from four countries
fragments.text: CBC in Canada, citing sources, reports Flávio Bolsonaro heading to the US after losing the election, and El Litoral in Argentina repeats the report from Brazil. SAPO in Portugal says allies of the senator expect Trump to grant him asylum, and Jornal de Brasília quotes a Mexican businessman saying he is travelling under protection. None of the headlines reports a statement from the US government.

fragments.label: The rest of the camp
fragments.text: Jornal de Brasília and Estado de Minas list other Bolsonaristas who have left Brazil, and O Globo runs a column saying the right must distance itself from the Bolsonaro family. Tarcísio, governor of São Paulo, says the election is over and Brazil goes on. El País English reports a Bolsonaro backtracking to say he will serve as Lula's opposition, which sits awkwardly beside the reports of departure.

fragments.label: Colombia and Venezuela
fragments.text: La Patria reports about 300 US soldiers arriving in Colombia for military exercises against drug trafficking. Clarín in Argentina says Corina Machado's return to Venezuela tests the limits of US influence. Hankyoreh in South Korea reads Lula's win as a blow to what it calls the 'Donroe Doctrine' and a brake on a rightward shift in Latin America.

fragments.label: Lula's warning
fragments.text: ANSA quotes Lula warning that 'there will be persecution' and that Brazil will defend its sovereignty. Nieuws.nl reports Brazil investigating foreign funding of the Bolsonaro campaign, without saying in the headline which country the money came from. Read beside the asylum reports, the sovereignty Lula says he will defend is sovereignty against pressure from Washington.

fragments.label: One actor in four roles
fragments.text: In these headlines the United States is a destination for a defeated Brazilian candidate, the reported source of protection for him, the sender of troops to Colombia and the measure against which Machado's homecoming is judged. The stories concern an election, a military exercise and an opposition leader's return in three different countries. Each outcome is being discussed in terms of what Washington will do.

fragments.label: Thin sourcing
fragments.text: The asylum story rests on the senator's allies, unnamed sources and a Mexican businessman. Brazilian politicians, the Bolsonaro family included, have long spent time in Florida, and a trip there after a defeat may be a private visit that opponents describe as flight. If no asylum is granted, the strongest link in this narrative disappears.

fragments.label: Routine programmes, local politics
fragments.text: US exercises in Colombia have run for decades under counter-narcotics agreements, and Machado's return is driven by Venezuelan politics. Joining them to a Brazilian election may reflect one Korean newspaper's 'Donroe Doctrine' framing more than any change in US policy. The collection also holds many Brazilian outlets, which makes the Bolsonaro departures look larger than they are.

horizons.label: How we got here: the past ten years
horizons.text: On 30 December 2022, two days before Lula's third inauguration, Jair Bolsonaro flew to Florida and stayed there for three months. On 8 January 2023 his supporters stormed the Congress, the Supreme Court and the presidential palace in Brasília, two years after the attack on the US Capitol. Brazil's Supreme Court convicted Bolsonaro of plotting a coup in September 2025, and the Trump administration had already imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods and sanctions on the judge Alexandre de Moraes, citing the case. His son Eduardo had moved to the United States earlier in 2025. In the same year US forces began striking boats in the Caribbean that Washington said carried drugs, and Corina Machado received the Nobel Peace Prize. By these headlines Lula has now won again, Flávio Bolsonaro is reported heading to the US with promises of asylum, and Estado de Minas counts him as one of several Bolsonaristas abroad. The decade turned the US from a place Brazilian politicians visited into a base for one side of Brazilian politics, the contested claim behind Lula's warning about persecution.

horizons.label: How we got here: the past fifty years
horizons.text: Brazil's military passed an amnesty law in 1979 and handed power to civilians in 1985, and the 1988 constitution followed. Unlike Argentina, which tried its juntas in 1985, Brazil prosecuted none of its generals, and the argument over that choice ran through the career of Jair Bolsonaro, who praised the dictatorship. The arrest of Augusto Pinochet in London in October 1998 on a Spanish warrant made the prosecution of former rulers possible across borders, so that leaving a country stopped being a reliable protection. In 2000 Washington and Bogotá began Plan Colombia, which made the US military a standing presence in Colombian counter-narcotics work; La Patria's report of about 300 US soldiers arriving for exercises continues that arrangement. Across the half-century the United States moved from backing military governments to backing elected ones it preferred, and Hankyoreh's phrase 'Donroe Doctrine' marks a view that policy is turning back. Others see the Colombian exercises and the Venezuelan file as long-running programmes with no new doctrine behind them.

horizons.label: How we got here: since September 2001
horizons.text: In June 2002, with the real falling before his first victory, Lula published a 'Letter to the Brazilian People' promising to honour contracts and debts, a reassurance aimed at markets and at Washington. In April of the same year a short-lived coup removed Hugo Chávez in Venezuela and was welcomed by the US government before it collapsed, which fixed Caracas's view of American intentions and is part of the frame in which Clarín now reads Machado's return. In 2013 documents leaked by Edward Snowden showed that the US National Security Agency had monitored President Dilma Rousseff's communications and Petrobras, and she called off a state visit to Washington. Sovereignty, the word Lula uses in ANSA's headline, has been the Brazilian left's term for that history since. Albert Hirschman's distinction between exit and voice describes the Bolsonaro camp's choices this week: Flávio's reported departure is exit, the El País report of a Bolsonaro promising to lead the opposition is voice, and the United States is the country that makes exit available.

horizons.label: How we got here: since 1945
horizons.text: The Monroe Doctrine of 1823 declared the Americas closed to European interference; after 1945 it became the frame for US action against governments in the hemisphere. Washington backed the overthrow of Jacobo Árbenz in Guatemala in 1954, welcomed the generals who removed João Goulart in Brazil in March 1964, and worked against Salvador Allende after his election in Chile in 1970. The same decades produced Latin America's own law of refuge. The Caracas Convention on Diplomatic Asylum of 1954 codified the regional practice of embassies sheltering defeated or pursued politicians, and exile in a neighbouring capital, or later in Miami, became a normal stage in many political careers. Flávio Bolsonaro's reported journey to the US 'under protection', in the words of a Mexican businessman quoted by Jornal de Brasília, belongs to that tradition, with the difference that the protecting state also imposes tariffs on Brazil and sends soldiers to Colombia. Whether an offer of asylum shelters a persecuted opponent or shields a politician from Brazilian courts is the point Lula and the Bolsonaros dispute.

readings.line: Patients in Canada, adult children in Germany and pharmacy users in India pay where public schemes fall short
readings.claim: In six countries this week a public scheme meant to cover a cost is reported as falling short, and in each the cost moves to a household. Canadians are paying for private surgery from savings and GoFundMe, German adult children are billed for their parents' care, Lucknow's subsidised generic pharmacies are short of medicines and a Bangladeshi antivenom programme lacks funds. Australia faces compensation claims from 50,000 people whose Centrelink payments were unlawfully suspended, and Mexicans enrolled in a voluntary pension scheme are asking what happens to them. The same question, who pays when the budget runs short, is being answered the same way in rich and poor states, which points to how these schemes are funded rather than to national wealth.

events.label: Canadians pay for private surgery
German children billed for parents' care
Lucknow generic pharmacies run short
Bangladesh antivenom production underfunded
Compensation for unlawful Centrelink suspensions
Mexican pension scheme rules in doubt

fragments.label: Canada
fragments.text: CBC Radio reports Canadians using their savings and GoFundMe campaigns to pay for private surgeries. Publicly insured operations in Canada are free at the point of use, so these patients are paying the full price. The headline does not give their reasons, but private payment there is normally a way around waiting lists.

fragments.label: India and Bangladesh
fragments.text: Amar Ujala reports a shortage of medicines at Lucknow's Jan Aushadhi Kendras, the government shops that sell generic drugs cheaply. bdnews24 reports that a Bangladeshi research centre is struggling for lack of funds and that its production of snake antivenom is uncertain. In both cases a public supply exists on paper, and a patient who finds it empty must buy elsewhere or go without.

fragments.label: Germany and Australia
fragments.text: Handelsblatt explains when adult children must pay for their parents' care costs. The ABC reports that 50,000 people could receive compensation for unlawful suspensions of Centrelink payments. In Germany the cost of care passes down a generation; in Australia it was carried by claimants whose payments stopped until the suspensions were found unlawful.

fragments.label: Mexico
fragments.text: Vanguardia asks what will happen to people already enrolled in IMSS Modality 40, the voluntary scheme through which workers pay extra contributions to raise their pension. Milenio publishes the November payment date for ISSSTE pensions. The first headline implies a change to the scheme without stating it, and those enrolled have paid in under rules that may move.

fragments.label: One shape in six countries
fragments.text: Each headline describes a public scheme that defines an entitlement, whether surgery, care, medicine, antivenom, income support or a pension, and a gap between that entitlement and what is delivered. In each the gap is filled by a household: savings and crowdfunding in Canada, children's income in Germany, private purchase in India and Bangladesh, lost payments in Australia and uncertainty for contributors in Mexico. The question being decided is who pays when the budget runs short, and the answer is the same in every case.

fragments.label: Rationing without a decision
fragments.text: None of these headlines reports a government announcing a cut. The rationing happens through queues, empty shelves, a laboratory without funds, a suspension applied by rule and a scheme change for those already enrolled. That makes the shift hard to see as policy and easy to treat as private misfortune, which is why it appears as advice columns, crowdfunding and city pages rather than as budget news.

fragments.label: Old stories, not a new shift
fragments.text: Canadian stories about private surgery and German stories about children paying for care have run for years, and Handelsblatt's piece is a wealth-advice column rather than a report of change. The ISSSTE headline is a routine payment notice. Without evidence that the gaps are widening this year, the narrative may be describing the permanent condition of any public scheme.

fragments.label: Different causes behind one shape
fragments.text: A Lucknow stock-out may be a distribution failure, a Bangladeshi laboratory's funding may turn on one grant, and the Australian story is about the state compensating people, which is a system correcting its own error. A shared shape is not a shared cause. Finding the same shape in six places may say more about the search than about any change in how these countries fund care.

horizons.label: How we got here: the past ten years
horizons.text: Between 2016 and 2019 Australia's Robodebt scheme used automated income matching to raise debts against welfare recipients; it was found unlawful, settled in 2020 and condemned by a royal commission in July 2023. The ABC's report that 50,000 people could be compensated for unlawful Centrelink suspensions is a second case in which a rule applied by machine stopped payments before a person checked them, the view from above that James C. Scott described. In Germany a 2020 law limited claims on adult children for their parents' care to those earning more than €100,000 a year, yet care home charges kept rising, which is why Handelsblatt still explains when children must pay. In Canada surgical backlogs grew during the pandemic, and Ontario passed a law in 2023 moving more procedures into private clinics; CBC's report of patients using savings and GoFundMe comes after that. India relaunched and expanded its generic pharmacy scheme in the mid-2010s. Across the decade governments kept the entitlements and changed the rules that decide who receives them and when.

horizons.label: How we got here: the past fifty years
horizons.text: In September 1978 the Alma-Ata declaration committed health ministers to 'health for all by the year 2000', with essential medicines at its centre; the World Health Organization had published its first essential medicines list in 1977. India's generic pharmacies and Bangladesh's antivenom work are late instruments of that idea, and bdnews24's report that antivenom production is uncertain for lack of funds shows how much it depends on yearly budgets. The Canada Health Act of 1984 barred extra billing for publicly insured services, so private surgery there is paid in full rather than topped up. Germany added compulsory long-term care insurance in 1995, designed to pay only part of the cost and leave the rest to savings, then social assistance, then children. Mexico reformed the IMSS pension system in 1997, moving new workers into individual accounts; Modality 40, the scheme Vanguardia reports on, lets those who contributed before July 1997 raise their pension under the old rules. Each design fixed a point where the state stopped paying and the household began.

horizons.label: How we got here: since September 2001
horizons.text: In June 2005 the Supreme Court of Canada ruled in Chaoulli v Quebec that a ban on private insurance for publicly covered services breached Quebec's charter where waiting times were too long, opening the legal argument behind the private clinics CBC's patients now use. In 2008 India launched its Jan Aushadhi scheme to sell generic medicines at low prices through dedicated shops, and Amar Ujala's report of shortages in Lucknow concerns those shops. Mexico created Seguro Popular in 2003 to cover people without social insurance, replaced it with INSABI in 2020 and folded that into IMSS-Bienestar in 2023, so patients had to learn a new system three times. Germany wrote a debt brake into its constitution in 2009, and Adam Tooze has described how, after the 2008 crisis, rich governments held down spending on services for most of a decade. The trajectory since 2001 has been to keep universal promises while changing the conditions of access, and courts and compensation schemes have become the places where the resulting gaps are argued.

horizons.label: How we got here: since 1945
horizons.text: The welfare states built after 1945 promised to remove from families the costs of illness and old age. Britain's National Health Service opened on 5 July 1948, and West Germany's 1957 pension reform tied pensions to wages. Saskatchewan introduced public hospital insurance in 1947 and medicare in 1962, the model for Canada's national Medical Care Act of 1966. Mexico founded the IMSS in 1943 and created ISSSTE for state employees in 1959, which is why Milenio still publishes ISSSTE's monthly payment dates. In 1946 the Bhore Committee recommended free state health services for all of India, a goal only partly met since. Tony Judt's Postwar describes these systems as part of a settlement between states and citizens after the war. The headlines in this narrative sit at the edges of that settlement seventy years on: the German family paying for care, the Canadian patient paying privately and the Indian pharmacy without stock are all where the postwar promise was limited from the start by budgets, means tests or the reach of the state.

readings.line: Nigeria's electoral body, New Zealand employers and an Australian court handle AI-made faces and files
readings.claim: Institutions that check whether a face or an application belongs to a real person are dealing with machine-made versions in several countries at once. Nigeria's electoral commission is investigating suspected AI-generated photos in the voters' register, New Zealand job seekers report being ignored as AI floods the job market, an Australian court has passed the first sentence under deepfake laws without jail, and fashion models face AI copies of their image. The mechanism is the same in each: producing a plausible picture or document now costs almost nothing, while checking it still takes a person's time. That gap is opening at once in elections, employment and the law of likeness.

events.label: Suspected AI photos in Nigeria's voter register
Applicants ignored as AI floods NZ jobs
First sentence under Australian deepfake laws
AI images and songs spread online
Arrest over edited video in Japan
Impersonation scams in Philippines and Ghana

rungs.label: A register, a job market, a court

fragments.label: Nigeria's register
fragments.text: Daily Post Nigeria reports that INEC, the electoral commission, is investigating suspected AI-generated photos in the voters' register. Other Nigerian headlines in the collection are already about the 2027 elections. A photograph in the register is meant to show that a voter exists.

fragments.label: New Zealand's job market
fragments.text: RNZ reports applicants being 'ghosted' as AI floods the job market. The headline leaves open whether the flood is of AI-written applications, AI screening by employers or both. In either case software stands at the point where each side expects to deal with a person.

fragments.label: Australia's first deepfake sentence
fragments.text: The Sydney Morning Herald reports that the first man sentenced under deepfake laws will not spend a day in jail. It is a first measure of how a court values the harm of making a false image of a real person.

fragments.label: Models, athletes and a song
fragments.text: bdnews24 reports that the fashion industry's AI boom threatens models' jobs and image rights. International Business Times UK reports an NBA player mocked for using AI to replace a friend in a photograph with someone else. In China, Sina asks readers what they think of an AI-made rap song that has spread across the internet.

fragments.label: Edited videos and impersonators
fragments.text: 47NEWS reports a man in Japan arrested on suspicion of editing a defamatory video, possibly with a YouTuber. The Philippine health department warns against scammers posing as its chief, and BBC News reports Ghanaian twins and a US woman pleading guilty to romance scams. These are older ways of faking a person, reported in the same week as the AI cases.

rungs.label: Cheap to make, costly to check

fragments.label: The mechanism
fragments.text: The voter register, the job application and the model's portfolio all depend on a check done by a person: an official comparing a face, a recruiter reading a letter, a client booking a known model. Generating a plausible photograph or letter now takes seconds, while checking it takes the same human time as before. When the inputs multiply and the checking does not, institutions either let fakes through, as INEC suspects, or stop replying, as RNZ's applicants describe.

fragments.label: Law made one case at a time
fragments.text: The responses so far are single cases rather than rules: one Australian sentence, one Japanese arrest, one Philippine warning. Image rights, which bdnews24 says are under threat, were written for a world in which using a person's likeness required that person or a photograph of them. The courts and police in these headlines are deciding what a copy of a person is worth without that assumption.

fragments.label: Not all of it is AI
fragments.text: The Nigerian photographs are only suspected to be generated. Three of the cases cited, the Japanese edited video, the Philippine impersonators and the Ghanaian romance fraud, use methods older than generative software. Grouping them under AI may follow a newsroom habit of labelling any fakery with the word of the moment.

fragments.label: An old complaint in new words
fragments.text: Job seekers complained of unanswered applications long before AI, and Nigerian voter registers have contained duplicate and invented names for decades. The narrative may be mistaking a familiar failure of overloaded institutions for a new mechanism because the headline now names AI. A light sentence in one Australian case is also too little to show how courts in general will treat the harm.

horizons.label: How we got here: the past ten years
horizons.text: The word deepfake came from a Reddit user in late 2017 who posted face-swapped pornography made with open-source software. Within five years image generators and chatbots had made synthetic pictures and text cheap for anyone, and ChatGPT reached a hundred million users within two months of its release in November 2022. Nigeria's electoral commission introduced the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System for the 2023 elections, matching fingerprints and faces at polling units, which assumes the registered photograph shows a real person; the Daily Post headline about suspected AI-generated photos in the register tests that assumption. Australia passed a federal law in 2024 making it a crime to share sexual deepfakes without consent, and the Sydney Morning Herald's report of a first sentence under deepfake laws, with no jail, shows how courts are starting to weigh it. Hiring went the same way, with employers adopting automated screening and applicants adopting generators, and RNZ's report of ghosted applicants describes both ends. The change across the decade was that producing a convincing image or letter came to cost less than verifying it.

horizons.label: How we got here: the past fifty years
horizons.text: Adobe released Photoshop in 1990, and for the first time a photograph could be altered on a desktop computer without a darkroom. In 1995 Netscape's listing put a price on the open internet, and the web became the place where pictures circulated with no record of where they came from. Nigeria returned to civilian rule in 1999 and has rebuilt its voters' register several times since, adding biometric data in 2011 because earlier registers held duplicate and invented names; the photographs INEC is now examining are the latest form of an old problem in that register. In fashion, the supermodel era of the 1980s and 1990s made a model's face a licensed commercial asset, which is why bdnews24's report treats AI copies as a threat to image rights as well as to jobs. Publicity rights, which American courts recognised from the 1950s, and European privacy law both assumed that a copy needed the person or a photograph of them. Generators remove that need, and the institutions built on it are being revised case by case.

horizons.label: How we got here: since September 2001
horizons.text: Facebook opened in 2004 and the iPhone went on sale in 2007, and within a decade billions of people had posted photographs of their own faces online, the material on which face generators are now trained. India began enrolling residents in the Aadhaar biometric identity system in 2010, and many states, Nigeria among them, followed with biometric voter and identity registers on the assumption that a body is harder to fake than a document. The same years saw organised online fraud grow, including romance scams of the kind the Ghanaian twins in BBC News's report admitted and impersonation of officials such as the Philippine health department now warns against. Shoshana Zuboff's account of platforms that profit from collecting personal data explains where the training images came from and why so few people were asked. The trajectory since 2001 is that identity checks moved from paper to the face in the same years that the face became easy to copy, and that is the position the Nigerian commission and New Zealand's employers now share.

horizons.label: How we got here: since 1945
horizons.text: In 1950 Alan Turing proposed the imitation game, in which a machine would count as thinking if a person could not tell its written answers from a human's. In 1956 a summer workshop at Dartmouth named the field artificial intelligence, funded by a foundation in a period when states paid for most research of that kind. Turing's test treated being mistaken for a person as the goal. The institutions in these headlines, an electoral commission, employers, courts and modelling agencies, are on the other side of that test and must tell machine output from human. Faking photographs is older than computing: Soviet censors removed purged officials such as Nikolai Yezhov from pictures in the late 1930s, but the work needed a state's darkrooms and staff. Marshall McLuhan argued in 1964 that each new medium changes the scale of what people can do. In this case the scale is that one person, such as the man Japanese police arrested on suspicion of editing a defamatory video, can now do what once took a ministry. The dispute is whether that is a new problem or an old one at lower cost.

readings.line: China dropped La Liga, an Indian court an Adani film, and a Korean drama faces calls to stop over Gwangju
readings.claim: In several countries this week a broadcast or publication is being removed, or demanded off air, because some party says it gives offence, and the party with the power to remove it is different each time. A Chinese platform dropped Racing-Real Madrid and La Liga broadcasts were suspended after a remark by Mbappé, an Indian court ordered a documentary on Adani and Modi taken down, a Korean drama faces calls to halt over a Gwangju episode, and Neil Young is suing to stop Trump rallies using his songs. Police in Jordan, Egypt and Spain are acting against content they call hateful or illegal, while a Mexican court struck down a state propaganda law. The shared question is who may decide what the public sees, and the answers run from a foreign ministry to a copyright holder.

events.label: China drops La Liga over Mbappé remark
Indian court orders Adani documentary removed
Calls to halt Korean drama over Gwangju
Police warn and detain over content
Neil Young sues over Trump rally music
Courts rule on speech in Mexico and Poland

fragments.label: La Liga in China
fragments.text: MARCA reports that China's leading content and internet platform has removed Racing-Real Madrid from its schedule. Hürriyet reports the Chinese foreign ministry reacting to a remark by Mbappé and La Liga broadcasts suspended, and El Colombiano says Mbappé has lost sponsors and been banned from a Chinese social network. None of the headlines in the collection says what he said.

fragments.label: A film in India, a drama in Korea
fragments.text: bdnews24 reports an Indian court ordering the takedown of a documentary on Adani and Modi. The Straits Times reports calls in South Korea to halt the drama Doctor X over an episode about Gwangju. In India a court has acted; in Korea the demand comes from outside the state, and the headline does not say who is making it.

fragments.label: Police action on content
fragments.text: Al-Anbat reports Jordan's security services saying they will not tolerate publishers of content that incites hatred or insults others. Masrawy reports Egypt's interior ministry seizing a Giza printing-press owner with 17,000 illegal publications. El Comercio reports a Spanish Instagrammer detained on suspicion of a hate crime over songs against immigrants, gay people, sick people and disabled people.

fragments.label: Courts and copyright
fragments.text: CBC reports Neil Young suing again because Trump rallies keep using his music. Milenio reports a Mexican court overturning a Veracruz law on government propaganda. Onet reports on President Karol Nawrocki's case against Onet itself, with Radosław Sikorski saying 'people knew'.

fragments.label: One question, many deciders
fragments.text: Each of these stories turns on whether some material may stay in public view, and each gives the decision to a different authority: a platform and a foreign ministry in China, a court in India, a campaign of objectors in Korea, a copyright holder in the US, and police in Jordan, Egypt and Spain. The grounds given are a claimed harm, to a nation's dignity, a company's reputation, a city's history or a group's safety. The act of removal is shared; what varies is who is entitled to carry it out.

fragments.label: Courts on both sides
fragments.text: The Mexican ruling against Veracruz's propaganda law shows a court limiting what a government may put before the public, the reverse of the Indian order. In Poland the president's case against Onet is being contested in public by the publisher's own journalists. The same week therefore holds removals ordered by courts and content laws struck down by them.

fragments.label: Different acts under one verb
fragments.text: China's removal of La Liga is a commercial and diplomatic reaction specific to its market, an Indian takedown order may be an ordinary defamation remedy, Korean calls to halt a drama have no legal force, and Neil Young is asserting a property right that most would call the opposite of censorship. The police actions in Jordan, Egypt and Spain apply ordinary criminal law. Putting them together because each ends with something taken down may join things that share only a word.

fragments.label: One story counted three times
fragments.text: Three of the headlines are the same Mbappé story told from Spain, Turkey and Colombia, and the narrative's reach depends on them. Without China and La Liga, what remains is a set of separate national disputes about speech of the kind reported every week. The collection's many Spanish-language sports outlets also make a football broadcasting dispute look larger than it is.

horizons.label: How we got here: the past ten years
horizons.text: In October 2019 the Houston Rockets' general manager posted support for Hong Kong's protesters and China's state broadcaster stopped showing Rockets games; in December CCTV dropped an Arsenal match after Mesut Özil criticised the treatment of Uyghurs. The Chinese platform that removed Racing-Real Madrid, and the suspension of La Liga broadcasts reported by Hürriyet after a remark by Mbappé, repeat that procedure. In India the government blocked links to the BBC documentary India: The Modi Question in January 2023 under emergency powers in the IT Rules of 2021, the same month Hindenburg Research accused the Adani group of fraud, which Adani denied; the court-ordered takedown of a documentary on Adani and Modi follows both. In South Korea SBS cancelled the drama Joseon Exorcist in March 2021 after two episodes over complaints of historical distortion, and the calls against Doctor X over Gwangju follow that campaign. The same years brought the toppling of Edward Colston's statue in Bristol in 2020 and other disputes over how the past is shown in public. Across the decade offence became grounds for removal organised by audiences and markets as well as by governments.

horizons.label: How we got here: the past fifty years
horizons.text: In May 1980 the army killed hundreds of people in Gwangju, and for most of the next decade Korean newspapers and television were barred from describing it as anything but a riot. After the 1987 democratic transition, a 1995 special law allowed prosecution, and in 1996 the former presidents Chun Doo-hwan and Roh Tae-woo were sentenced for the 1979 coup and the killings, then pardoned the following year. The official account of Gwangju reversed: what censors once removed became the history that objectors now say a drama such as Doctor X distorts. Films such as A Taxi Driver in 2017 carried that account to a mass audience. In the same decades television became the main market for football. The Premier League's 1992 deal with satellite television turned a national league into a product sold abroad, Spanish football followed, and so a Chinese platform's schedule now matters to Racing and Real Madrid. In both lines the removal of a broadcast became the sanction available to whoever controls the screen.

horizons.label: How we got here: since September 2001
horizons.text: In September 2005 the Danish newspaper Jyllands-Posten published cartoons of the Prophet Muhammad, and the protests and boycotts of early 2006 made offence to a community a matter for foreign ministries and trade. Since then laws against hate speech online have multiplied, and the Jordanian security statement and the Spanish arrest of an Instagrammer over songs against immigrants and disabled people are applications of such laws. Courts have also limited them. In 2015 India's Supreme Court struck down section 66A of the Information Technology Act in the Shreya Singhal case as too vague, while leaving the government's blocking powers in place. Mexico's ruling against a Veracruz propaganda law belongs to the same practice of judicial review. Musicians used a different tool. Jackson Browne sued John McCain's campaign in 2008 over a song in an advertisement, and Neil Young objected when Trump used Rockin' in the Free World in 2015 and sued in 2020; the CBC headline says he is suing again. Since 2001 the same act, removing content, has come to be carried out under many separate legal regimes at once.

horizons.label: How we got here: since 1945
horizons.text: After 1945 most states treated broadcasting as a national institution, licensed or owned by government. The first European Cup in 1955, carried in its later seasons by the Eurovision network, made football one of the first things Europeans watched together across borders, and televised World Cups made the national team something a nation watched at the same hour, in the sense Benedict Anderson described for newspapers. Control of the screen was a state function. Spain had no private television until a law of 1988, and in Mexico the government's hold on the press was such that the army's killing of students at Tlatelolco in October 1968 was barely reported at the time. The Veracruz law on government propaganda that a Mexican court has now overturned, whose terms the headline does not give, belongs to that long argument over official messaging. The difference in 2026 is that the power to remove is held by a foreign platform, a court, a copyright holder or a police unit, as well as by governments over their own broadcasters.
